bibl.title: Local category-specific gamma band responses in the visual cortex do not reflect conscious perception
bibl.publisher: The Journal of Neuroscience: The Official Journal of the Society for Neuroscience

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether category-specific gamma band responses in higher-order visual cortex are a direct neural correlate of conscious perception or a prerequisite for it
span.quote: Here we directly address this issue by developing a new experimental paradigm in which conscious perception is modulated either by sensory evidence or by previous exposure of the images while recording intracranial EEG from the higher-order visual cortex of human epilepsy patients.

span.label: if local gamma band responses reflect conscious perception, do they follow it however it is brought about
span.quote: A clear prediction is that neural processes directly reflecting conscious perception should be present regardless of how it comes about.

span.label: shows that two manipulations which raise conscious perception equally are not equally reflected in gamma band responses — only sensory evidence is — and concludes local gamma is not the correlate of consciousness
span.quote: In contrast, we observed that although subjective reports were modulated both by sensory evidence and by previous exposure, gamma band responses solely reflected sensory evidence.

span.label: null-result
span.quote: In contrast, we observed that although subjective reports were modulated both by sensory evidence and by previous exposure, gamma band responses solely reflected sensory evidence.

span.label: neural correlates of conscious visual perception
span.quote: One central controversy in consciousness research is whether conscious perception arises locally from activity in sensory cortices ( Zeki, 2001 ; Malach, 2007 ) or whether it requires integration across brain areas ( Tononi and Koch, 2008 ; Melloni and Singer, 2010 ; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011 ).

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Here we directly address this issue by developing a new experimental paradigm in which conscious perception is modulated either by sensory evidence or by previous exposure of the images while recording intracranial EEG from the higher-order visual cortex of human epilepsy patients.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Category-specific gamma indexes local sensory processing that is a necessary precondition for conscious perception rather than its direct correlate
span.quote: Thus, an alternative explanation for the findings of Fisch et al. (2009) is that category-specific GBRs in sensory cortices reflect local processing, which is a necessary prerequisite for but not the direct correlate of conscious perception.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Stronger local preprocessing raises the probability that a stimulus reaches awareness, which manufactures a correlation between gamma and 'seen' reports without gamma causing awareness
span.quote: In other words, in a paradigm such as used by Fisch et al. (2009) , it cannot be ruled out that the enhanced GBR just reflected more effective preprocessing of stimuli that enhanced the chances of these stimuli to get perceived consciously.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Differences in unconscious local processing propagate into different conscious outcomes, so local responses can correlate with awareness while being prerequisites of it
span.quote: In typical experimental paradigms, differences in local unconscious processing might lead to different outcomes regarding conscious perception, and therefore, specific local responses can correlate with conscious perception without necessarily being direct correlates of conscious experience.

span.label: the criterion is invariance, not correlation: a correlate of consciousness must move whenever consciousness moves, whatever moved it
span.quote: A clear prediction is that neural processes directly reflecting conscious perception should be present regardless of how it comes about.

span.label: the disconfirmation rests on that invariance failing, which is why a single dissociation is enough to reject the proposal
span.quote: It is this lack of invariance of the local GBR that makes it unlikely that GBR reflect a mechanism directly responsible for conscious perception.

span.label: two routes to the same behavioural endpoint are engineered — one that runs through local processing and one that does not — so the neural measure can be asked to choose
span.quote: we manipulated conscious perception in two different ways: either by changing the amount of sensory evidence, which directly modulates local processing, or by previously exposing the patients to the pictures before the test phase (i.e., providing prior knowledge), which is a factor less dependent on local processing

span.label: the equivalence of the two routes is established behaviourally first, across three separate samples, because the whole argument collapses if one manipulation is simply stronger
span.quote: Both factors boosted subjective reports similarly ( t (5) = 1.510, p = 0.191), which is also corroborated by the absence of an interaction of these factors ( p > 0.9).

span.label: the null is defended by Monte Carlo power simulation rather than asserted, showing the test would have caught a 30% shift
span.quote: Trials were randomly assigned into two groups; 30% of the mean of the original distribution was added to one group to mimic the shift due to an experimental factor followed by a Wilcoxon test between the groups.

span.label: the electrode selection contrast is chosen so that neither experimental factor can contaminate it — same degradation, neither group previously seen
span.quote: Importantly, this comparison was neither confounded by previous exposure (as none of the picture groups had been seen before) nor by sensory evidence (as both picture groups shared the same level of degradation), enabling the extraction of person-specific signatures independently of the experimental factors.

span.label: the disputed study's own frequency band is analysed unchanged so the comparison is direct, and only then extended
span.quote: We thus tested the same frequency range to allow direct comparisons between studies.

span.label: catch trials containing only background give an independent check that the subjective report is trustworthy before it is used as the criterion
span.quote: The low number of false alarms in the 44 catch trials (mean 1.5, SD 2.3) ensures that the subjects' visibility judgments were reliable.

span.label: the rival explanation for the null — repetition suppression cancelling an enhancement — is closed with a boundary condition from the literature: repetition of degraded images enhances rather than suppresses
span.quote: However, repetition suppression is typically observed only when the same, un-degraded image is repeated, while repetition leads to enhancement when degraded images are repeated ( Müller et al., 2012 ).

span.label: images are rotated through every condition across patients so no result can be an artefact of particular pictures
span.quote: To rule out any picture-specific effects in the neural measures, we pseudorandomized the pictures containing a person such that across four patients, each picture was assigned to every condition exactly one time.

span.label: the within-subject reply to 'sensory evidence is just stronger' is that even patients for whom exposure mattered more behaviourally showed only the sensory effect neurally
span.quote: Moreover, even in those subjects where previous exposure had a numerically stronger impact on perception than sensory evidence, GBR was exclusively modulated by the latter.

span.label: Electrode coverage did not permit testing the alternative account, that long-range integration rather than local gamma tracks conscious perception.
span.quote: Due to limitations in the electrode coverage, we were unable to test this prediction in the current study.

span.label: Whether the two manipulations affect interareal integration in the same way is left open.
span.quote: It remains an open question whether sensory evidence and previous exposure similarly enhance interareal integration ( Melloni et al., 2007 ; Gaillard et al., 2009 ).

span.label: the alternative the paper favours — long-range integration — could not be tested with the electrodes available
span.quote: Due to limitations in the electrode coverage, we were unable to test this prediction in the current study.

span.label: whether the two manipulations affect interareal integration equally is unknown, so the positive account is untested
span.quote: It remains an open question whether sensory evidence and previous exposure similarly enhance interareal integration ( Melloni et al., 2007 ; Gaillard et al., 2009 ).

span.label: only one electrode showed a low-gamma effect surviving correction, so the low-band comparison with the disputed study rests on uncorrected effects
span.quote: In the lGBR range, only one electrode showed person-specific effects that survived the correction for multiple comparisons.

span.label: the frequency comparison with the disputed study is partly inference, since that study did not analyse above 70 Hz
span.quote: As there was no visible indication of attenuation in power in Fisch et al. (2009) , it is likely that higher frequencies exhibited a similar response.

span.label: full randomisation held for only four of the six patients
span.quote: Although we report data from six patients, results are comparable when restricting the analysis to four subjects with a complete randomization.

span.label: the integration account is left standing rather than supported, pending paradigms of this kind applied to it
span.quote: Until the relationship between long-range integration and conscious perception is not disputed by experimental paradigms like ours, such interareal interactions remain a viable candidate for mediating conscious perception.

span.label: Morlet wavelet convolution at roughly six cycles, used to resolve gamma power in time without committing to fixed epochs
span.quote: For each trial, bipolar derivations were analyzed in the time–frequency domain by convolution with complex Gaussian Morlet wavelets with a bandwidth parameter f 0 /σ f = 6, i.e., wavelets of approximately six cycles length.

span.label: Monte Carlo resampling used not to test the hypothesis but to establish that the reported null had the power to have found an effect
span.quote: Post hoc power analysis was done with Monte Carlo simulations.

span.label: false discovery rate control applied across the full electrode-by-time grid, which is what lets the per-electrode table be read as a whole
span.quote: Results were corrected for multiple comparisons using false discovery rate across all time windows and electrodes.

span.label: the pictures containing a person were PSEUDORANDOMISED across four patients, so that each picture was assigned to every condition exactly once
span.quote: To rule out any picture-specific effects in the neural measures, we pseudorandomized the pictures containing a person such that across four patients, each picture was assigned to every condition exactly one time.

span.label: neural correlate — as anything that covaries with report, versus as the process uniquely and directly associated with the experience; the paper's whole case turns on the second
span.quote: the methods commonly used for studying the neural correlates of consciousness are not specific for conscious experience but may reflect processes that precede or follow it

span.label: gamma band response — low (30–70 Hz) versus high (70–150 Hz); the paper argues they are one broadband process seen more strongly at high frequencies
span.quote: Thus, hGBR and lGBR may reflect a similar process, which is stronger at higher frequencies.

span.label: conscious perception — as the subjective report of seeing versus as the objective gender discrimination; both are collected and the analysis rests on the first
span.quote: Our analysis focuses on the subjective task, as our goal was to address the neural profile that correlates with subjective reports about conscious perception.

span.label: enhancing perception — by adding stimulus information versus by adding prior knowledge; behaviourally equivalent here, neurally not
span.quote: Perception appears to be modulated equally by previous exposure and sensory evidence, but this effect manifests itself in the local GBR only in the case of sensory evidence.

span.label: consciousness arising locally in sensory cortices versus requiring integration across areas — the controversy the paper is intervening in
span.quote: One central controversy in consciousness research is whether conscious perception arises locally from activity in sensory cortices ( Zeki, 2001 ; Malach, 2007 ) or whether it requires integration across brain areas ( Tononi and Koch, 2008 ; Melloni and Singer, 2010 ; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011 ).

span.label: an effect that is corrected across electrodes and times versus one that is uncorrected; Table 1 reports both and the argument uses them differently
span.quote: Asterisks indicate corrected effects across electrodes/times.

span.label: contradicts → Fisch et al. (2009), the finding that local category-specific gamma band responses in visual cortex mark conscious perception
span.quote: What could be the reasons for the discrepancy between our results and those obtained by Fisch et al. (2009) from which these authors concluded that local category-specific GBR are markers of conscious perception?

span.label: builds-on → Fisch et al. (2009) - electrode-selection procedure and analysed frequency range adopted for direct comparability
span.quote: Category-specific electrodes were determined following a procedure similar to Fisch et al. (2009)

span.label: replicates → Fisch et al. (2009) - the contrastive seen-versus-unseen gamma band enhancement
span.quote: In line with Fisch et al. (2009) , we observed a strong and sustained GBR that outlasted the stimulus presentation (150 ms) when subjects reported having perceived the person in the picture.

span.label: builds-on → Aru et al. (2012) and de Graaf et al. (2012), the argument that standard NCC methods confound prerequisites and consequences of consciousness
span.quote: This obvious discrepancy might be resolved when considering a recently uncovered theoretical problem that states that the methods commonly used for studying the neural correlates of consciousness are not specific for conscious experience but may reflect processes that precede or follow it ( Aru et al., 2012 ; de Graaf et al., 2012 ).

span.label: contradicts → Fisch et al. (2009), that category-specific gamma in visual cortex correlates with and marks conscious perception
span.quote: Fisch and colleagues (2009) showed that category-specific gamma band responses (GBR) in the visual cortex correlate with conscious perception.

span.label: critiques → the contrastive method as used throughout consciousness research
span.quote: It has been remarked previously that the contrastive method, i.e., the direct comparison between trials with and without conscious recognition, does not exclusively reflect neural processes directly and uniquely associated with conscious experience of the target but also those that precede or follow conscious experience ( Aru et al., 2012 ; de Graaf et al., 2012 ).

span.label: supports → theories grounding consciousness in long-range integration rather than local processing depth
span.quote: Numerous contemporary theories of consciousness propose that conscious experience is not related to the depth of local cortical processing but is grounded in long-range integration across brain areas ( Tononi and Koch, 2008 ; Melloni and Singer, 2010 ; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011 ).

span.label: builds-on → Gray and Singer (1989), that stimulus-specific gamma persists under anesthesia
span.quote: This idea is consistent with the classic findings showing strong local stimulus-specific gamma band activity even under anesthesia ( Gray and Singer, 1989 ).

span.label: critiques → neuroimaging evidence for local accounts, as too slow to see the dynamics at issue
span.quote: Empirical support for the idea that conscious perception is reflected in activity of sensory areas mostly stems from neuroimaging studies ( Grill-Spector et al., 2000 ; Hesselmann et al., 2011 ), which are insensitive to the neural dynamics underlying the perceptual effects.

span.label: extends → the authors' own theoretical critique of NCC methodology (Aru et al., 2012), by turning it into an experiment
span.quote: By going beyond the contrastive analysis, we could directly test pivotal predictions arising from the experimental work of others ( Fisch et al., 2009 ) and dissect neural processes that precede consciousness from those that are unique for consciousness.

span.label: gamma band responses —distinct-from→ neural correlates of consciousness
span.quote: This result contradicts the proposal that local gamma band responses in the higher-order visual cortex reflect conscious perception.

span.label: gamma band responses —is-a→ prerequisites
span.quote: Thus, an alternative explanation for the findings of Fisch et al. (2009) is that category-specific GBRs in sensory cortices reflect local processing, which is a necessary prerequisite for but not the direct correlate of conscious perception.

span.label: sensory evidence —contrasted-with→ previous exposure
span.quote: Two experimental factors controlled the images' visibility: sensory evidence and previous exposure ( Fig. 1 A ).

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · sensory evidence —causes→ gamma band responses
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span said hGBR rather than the endpoint's own name. This sentence names both and states the dependence in its careful form - gamma band responses 'SOLELY reflected sensory evidence', while subjective reports were modulated by two things. — strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: We observed that hGBR was significantly higher when sensory evidence was stronger ( Fig. 3 B ).

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED FROM A NEITHER-ENDPOINT SPAN) · previous exposure —causes→ conscious perception
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED FROM A NEITHER-ENDPOINT SPAN. The old span named neither term - it described what subjects reported. This sentence names both and states the DESIGN: 'a new experimental paradigm in which CONSCIOUS PERCEPTION is modulated either by sensory evidence or by PREVIOUS EXPOSURE of the images'. The causal claim is the manipulation, not an observed association. — strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: subjects reported to perceive the person on the degraded picture more often when pictures had either lower degradation ( F (1,5) = 25.626, p = 0.004) or when subjects were previously exposed to the clear version of the picture ( F (1,5) = 7.463, p = 0.041) ( Fig. 1 B )

span.label: previous exposure —operationalised-as→ prior knowledge
span.quote: The familiarization phase aimed at establishing prior knowledge by exposing half of the pictures subsequently shown in the test phase.

span.label: sensory evidence —operationalised-as→ degradation
span.quote: Sensory evidence was varied by presenting images at two degradation levels (high and low noise).

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · conscious perception —operationalised-as→ subjective task
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span described the subjective task without naming conscious perception. This sentence names both and says WHY the task stands for the concept: it addresses the neural profile correlating with subjective reports about conscious perception. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: In the subjective task, subjects reported whether they had seen a person in the picture.

span.label: long-range integration —same-as→ neural correlates of consciousness
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak
span.quote: Numerous contemporary theories of consciousness propose that conscious experience is not related to the depth of local cortical processing but is grounded in long-range integration across brain areas ( Tononi and Koch, 2008 ; Melloni and Singer, 2010 ; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011 ).

span.label: RETRACTED (`PART OF THE SAME X` IS `part-of`, AND THE SCHEMA HAS THAT TYPE) · hGBR —same-as→ lGBR
span.note: RETRACTED: `PART OF THE SAME X` IS `part-of`, AND THE SCHEMA HAS THAT TYPE. The edge is `hGBR --same-as--> lGBR`. The span: 'SUGGESTING THAT lGBR and hGBR ARE PART OF THE SAME BROADBAND PROCESS.' Two things being parts of one process does not make them each other - and the relation the sentence states is available in the vocabulary, as two `part-of` edges to the broadband process, which would also preserve the third term the identity edge deletes. THE AUTHOR DECLINES THE IDENTITY IN THE SAME BREATH, and the tag is stronger than the sentence it quotes. `Suggesting` is the authors reporting what a figure is consistent with, not what they have shown. — strength of the relation: 0.8
span.quote: Figure 2 shows that the differences between pictures containing a person and those with only background started at ∼50 Hz and continued throughout higher frequencies, suggesting that lGBR and hGBR are part of the same broadband process.

span.label: person-selective —operationalised-as→ catch images
span.quote: An electrode was considered person-selective if significantly higher GBR were observed for pictures containing a person in the foreground (from the condition low sensory evidence and without previous exposure) than for those only containing the background (catch images) in the interval 100–500 ms poststimulus presentation.

span.label: gamma band responses —distinct-from→ conscious perception
span.quote: In fact, early studies have shown that such local stimulus-specific increases in gamma band activity are observed even under anesthesia ( Gray and Singer, 1989 ) and might thus reflect low-level unconscious processing that precedes conscious experience.

span.label: fusiform gyrus —part-of→ visual cortex
span.quote: Person-specific enhancement of hGBR was observed on seven electrodes belonging to five different patients, which all were localized on the surface of the lateral occipital cortex and fusiform gyrus, in good agreement with the localization of the body-selective areas of the human brain ( Table 1 ) ( Peelen and Downing, 2007 ).

span.label: conscious perception —operationalised-as→ subjective task
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — RE-GROUNDS Aru2012-local-category-specific-gamma-band-responses[7]: the old span named ONE endpoint.
span.quote: Our analysis focuses on the subjective task, as our goal was to address the neural profile that correlates with subjective reports about conscious perception.

span.label: sensory evidence —causes→ gamma band responses
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — RE-GROUNDS Aru2012-local-category-specific-gamma-band-responses[3]: the old span named ONE endpoint.
span.quote: In contrast, we observed that although subjective reports were modulated both by sensory evidence and by previous exposure, gamma band responses solely reflected sensory evidence.

span.label: previous exposure —causes→ conscious perception
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — RE-GROUNDS Aru2012-local-category-specific-gamma-band-responses[4]: the old span named NEITHER endpoint.
span.quote: Here we directly address this issue by developing a new experimental paradigm in which conscious perception is modulated either by sensory evidence or by previous exposure of the images while recording intracranial EEG from the higher-order visual cortex of human epilepsy patients.

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: The percentage of “seen” responses in the subjective task was analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA with factors previous exposure (previously exposed vs novel) and sensory evidence (high vs low degradation).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Even with this fine-scale perceptual task, both previous exposure ( F (1,7) = 53.072, p = 1.65E−4) and sensory evidence ( F (1,7) = 23.526, p = 0.002) modulated perception similarly ( t test on the difference of the effects: t (7) = 0.237, p = 0.891).

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
span.quote: whereby the single-trial time courses of the lGBR and hGBR were subjected to a nonparametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test contrasting factors: sensory evidence, previous exposure, and visibility.

span.label: false discovery rate correction
span.quote: Results were corrected for multiple comparisons using false discovery rate across all time windows and electrodes.

span.label: Monte Carlo simulation
span.quote: Post hoc power analysis was done with Monte Carlo simulations.

span.label: statistical power
span.quote: Here power corresponds to the proportion of comparisons the Wilcoxon test correctly identifies

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: B , Proportion of “seen” person trials in the four experimental conditions. Error bars indicate SEM.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: The low number of false alarms in the 44 catch trials (mean 1.5, SD 2.3) ensures that the subjects' visibility judgments were reliable.

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: The percentage of “seen” responses in the subjective task was analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA with factors previous exposure (previously exposed vs novel) and sensory evidence (high vs low degradation).

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
span.quote: the single-trial time courses of the lGBR and hGBR were subjected to a nonparametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test contrasting factors: sensory evidence, previous exposure, and visibility

span.label: false discovery rate
span.quote: Results were corrected for multiple comparisons using false discovery rate across all time windows and electrodes.

span.label: Post hoc power analysis
span.quote: Post hoc power analysis was done with Monte Carlo simulations.

span.label: Monte Carlo simulations
span.quote: This was repeated 10,000 times.

span.label: F
SEM
span.quote: Error bars indicate SEM.

span.label: Both experimental routes to conscious perception worked: reducing image degradation and having previously seen the image each raised the rate of 'seen' reports.
span.quote: In the group of six patients, sensory evidence and previous exposure both modulated the visibility of the persons on the pictures

span.label: The two manipulations boosted subjective visibility to a statistically indistinguishable degree and did not interact.
span.quote: Both factors boosted subjective reports similarly ( t (5) = 1.510, p = 0.191), which is also corroborated by the absence of an interaction of these factors

span.label: The equality of the two effects on perception replicated in a larger sample of healthy controls.
span.quote: Here, both previous exposure ( F (1,23) = 70.167, p = 1.93E−8) and sensory evidence ( F (1,23) = 69.109, p = 2.21E−8) had a significant effect on subjective perception.

span.label: Category-specific gamma responses were larger on trials where the person was reported seen, replicating the earlier result the study set out to test.
span.quote: In line with Fisch et al. (2009) , we observed a strong and sustained GBR that outlasted the stimulus presentation (150 ms) when subjects reported having perceived the person in the picture.

span.label: The critical dissociation: gamma responses tracked sensory evidence but were completely unaffected by previous exposure, even though both equally enhanced conscious perception.
span.quote: hGBR was significantly modulated by sensory evidence in 85% (6/7) of the person-specific electrodes in four different patients, but none of them showed an effect of previous exposure

span.label: A post hoc power analysis showed the null effect of previous exposure was not a detection failure.
span.quote: Power analysis revealed that the mean power of our test over the seven electrodes and eight time windows was 0.94 and 0.9 for a 30% change at the uncorrected and corrected level, respectively, confirming the robustness of our methods to detect a potential effect of previous exposure.

span.label: Low and high gamma effects formed one continuous broadband response starting near 50 Hz rather than two distinct phenomena.
span.quote: Figure 2 shows that the differences between pictures containing a person and those with only background started at ∼50 Hz and continued throughout higher frequencies, suggesting that lGBR and hGBR are part of the same broadband process.

span.label: Because local gamma does not track conscious perception invariantly across the two routes to it, it cannot be the mechanism directly responsible for conscious perception.
span.quote: It is this lack of invariance of the local GBR that makes it unlikely that GBR reflect a mechanism directly responsible for conscious perception.

span.label: both lower degradation and prior exposure raised the proportion of trials where a person was reported seen
span.quote: subjects reported to perceive the person on the degraded picture more often when pictures had either lower degradation ( F (1,5) = 25.626, p = 0.004) or when subjects were previously exposed to the clear version of the picture ( F (1,5) = 7.463, p = 0.041) ( Fig. 1 B )

span.label: the two manipulations boosted subjective perception to a statistically indistinguishable degree, with no interaction
span.quote: Both factors boosted subjective reports similarly ( t (5) = 1.510, p = 0.191), which is also corroborated by the absence of an interaction of these factors ( p > 0.9).

span.label: the behavioural equivalence replicated in 24 healthy controls, again with no interaction
span.quote: Here, both previous exposure ( F (1,23) = 70.167, p = 1.93E−8) and sensory evidence ( F (1,23) = 69.109, p = 2.21E−8) had a significant effect on subjective perception.

span.label: and again in eight subjects using an 11-point perceptual rating scale rather than a yes/no report
span.quote: Even with this fine-scale perceptual task, both previous exposure ( F (1,7) = 53.072, p = 1.65E−4) and sensory evidence ( F (1,7) = 23.526, p = 0.002) modulated perception similarly ( t test on the difference of the effects: t (7) = 0.237, p = 0.891).

span.label: gamma tracked sensory evidence on 6 of 7 person-specific electrodes and prior exposure on none
span.quote: hGBR was significantly modulated by sensory evidence in 85% (6/7) of the person-specific electrodes in four different patients, but none of them showed an effect of previous exposure ( Fig. 3 C ).

span.label: the population analysis agreed: sensory evidence significant from 100 to 450 ms, previous exposure at p > 0.2 in every window
span.quote: These results were confirmed by the population analysis, where we only observed effects of sensory evidence ( p < 0.05, 100–450 ms poststimulus, except for 150–200 ms, where p = 0.053) but not of previous exposure ( p > 0.2 for all time windows).

span.label: the null was not a power failure — the test had 0.94 power to detect a 30% change uncorrected, 0.9 corrected
span.quote: Power analysis revealed that the mean power of our test over the seven electrodes and eight time windows was 0.94 and 0.9 for a 30% change at the uncorrected and corrected level, respectively, confirming the robustness of our methods to detect a potential effect of previous exposure.

span.label: the paper did replicate the original positive result: gamma was higher on trials where the person was consciously perceived, on 5 of 7 electrodes
span.quote: In line with Fisch et al. (2009) , we observed a strong and sustained GBR that outlasted the stimulus presentation (150 ms) when subjects reported having perceived the person in the picture. This was observed in 70% (5/7) of the person-specific electrodes in four different patients.

span.label: person-specific gamma appeared on 7 electrodes across 5 patients, all on lateral occipital cortex and fusiform gyrus
span.quote: Person-specific enhancement of hGBR was observed on seven electrodes belonging to five different patients, which all were localized on the surface of the lateral occipital cortex and fusiform gyrus, in good agreement with the localization of the body-selective areas of the human brain ( Table 1 ) ( Peelen and Downing, 2007 ).

span.label: the person-vs-background difference ran from about 50 Hz upward, indicating one broadband process rather than two bands
span.quote: Figure 2 shows that the differences between pictures containing a person and those with only background started at ∼50 Hz and continued throughout higher frequencies, suggesting that lGBR and hGBR are part of the same broadband process.

span.label: false alarms on background-only catch trials averaged 1.5 of 44, so the visibility reports were reliable
span.quote: The low number of false alarms in the 44 catch trials (mean 1.5, SD 2.3) ensures that the subjects' visibility judgments were reliable.

span.label: neural correlates of consciousness (NCC), local view
span.term: neural correlates of consciousness (NCC), local view
span.quote: One theoretical view argues that the neural correlates of consciousness (NCC) reside in local activity in sensory cortices.

span.label: low and high gamma band responses (lGBR / hGBR)
span.term: low and high gamma band responses (lGBR / hGBR)
span.quote: We analyzed GBR in two frequency ranges: low (30–70 Hz, lGBR) and high GBR (70–150 Hz, hGBR).

span.label: person-selective electrode
span.quote: An electrode was considered person-selective if significantly higher GBR were observed for pictures containing a person in the foreground (from the condition low sensory evidence and without previous exposure) than for those only containing the background (catch images) in the interval 100–500 ms poststimulus presentation.

span.label: contrastive method
span.quote: It has been remarked previously that the contrastive method, i.e., the direct comparison between trials with and without conscious recognition, does not exclusively reflect neural processes directly and uniquely associated with conscious experience of the target but also those that precede or follow conscious experience

span.label: statistical power (as operationalised here)
span.quote: Here power corresponds to the proportion of comparisons the Wilcoxon test correctly identifies

span.label: person-selective
span.quote: An electrode was considered person-selective if significantly higher GBR were observed for pictures containing a person in the foreground (from the condition low sensory evidence and without previous exposure) than for those only containing the background (catch images) in the interval 100–500 ms poststimulus presentation.

span.label: contrastive method
span.quote: the contrastive method, i.e., the direct comparison between trials with and without conscious recognition

span.label: Sensory evidence
span.quote: Sensory evidence was varied by presenting images at two degradation levels (high and low noise).

span.label: Previous exposure
span.quote: Previous exposure was varied by either showing previously exposed or new images, for which no preexisting memory had been established.

span.label: power
span.quote: Here power corresponds to the proportion of comparisons the Wilcoxon test correctly identifies as “different.”

span.label: familiarization phase
span.quote: The familiarization phase aimed at establishing prior knowledge by exposing half of the pictures subsequently shown in the test phase.

span.label: sensory evidence (image degradation level)
span.quote: Sensory evidence was varied by presenting images at two degradation levels

span.label: previous exposure (prior knowledge of the image)
span.term: previous exposure (prior knowledge of the image)
span.quote: Previous exposure was varied by either showing previously exposed or new images, for which no preexisting memory had been established.

span.label: percentage of 'seen' responses in the subjective task
span.term: percentage of 'seen' responses in the subjective task
span.quote: The percentage of “seen” responses in the subjective task was analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA with factors previous exposure (previously exposed vs novel) and sensory evidence (high vs low degradation).
